set.hook: Signless Barceloneta tavern from 1944, the kitchen that first fried la bomba.
set.why: The family opened in 1944 behind a door with no sign, feeding dockers and fishermen from a stove by the entrance. In the 1950s the grandmother, María, rolled spiced meat inside mashed potato, fried it, and topped it with allioli and a red picante; the bomba spread across the city, and the recipe never left the house. Palmira Solé, who married into the family in 1955, still cooks; the bombas often run out by early afternoon.

set.hook: A Raval dairy-bar since 1870, where the Viaders invented Cacaolat; now in the fifth generation's hands.
set.why: Rafaela Coma opened a dairy here in 1870 and the Viaders took it over around 1904. In 1931 Joan Viader Roger tasted a cold chocolate milk at the Budapest fair and patented his own at home that December: Cacaolat, a brand the family sold long ago. On 7 May 2026 Marc Espuny Casademunt became owner, a month before his mother, Mercè Casademunt Viader, retired at 67, ending fears the granja would close with her.

set.hook: A Gothic Quarter shop selling sweets made in Spanish convents, with a café in the vaults below.

Ferran Adrià calls it a magical place. In 2025 it turned 80, and Time Out reported the bar marking the anniversary by inviting people in to eat.

set.hook: A standing-room cava bar by Port Vell, pouring its own pink cava since 1969.
set.why: Since 1969 this narrow room off Port Vell has sold its own cava, made under the Berenguer Ramon label, at the counter and by the bottle in the shop. There are no stools: you stand with a glass of the pink rosat and a hot botifarra bocadillo from the grill, while hams hang overhead. The house rosat semi-sec is also sold by Barcelona wine retailers, so the bar doubles as the cellar door for its own wine.

set.hook: The Born burger counter that started Barcelona's gourmet-burger run in 2010; now part of AmRest.
set.why: Brad Ainsworth opened Bacoa in 2010 as a 15-seat burger bar behind the Santa Caterina market, grilling patties over stone and winning Time Out Barcelona's best-sandwich award that year. In 2018 AmRest, the group behind Burger King and Pizza Hut in Spain, bought the chain for about EUR 3.7 million; its two own sites were the Kiosko on Marquès de l'Argentera 1 and Colomines 2, the second since listed as closed.

set.hook: A 1970 white-banquette tortilla room under life-size photo silhouettes of Karin Leiz.
set.why: Photographer Leopoldo Pomés opened Flash Flash in 1970 with architect Alfonso Milà, who designed the white leather room with Federico Correa. The black-and-white figures on the walls are cut from Pomés's photographs of the model Karin Leiz, the same figure from his advertising work. The kitchen turns out more than fifty tortillas, and the room has changed so little that it reached its fiftieth birthday in 2020 still looking like 1970.

counters.title: Eating at the stove's edge
counters.story: Barcelona's best tapas counters put the diner a stool's width from the cook, and the meal is part watching. At Bar Cañete on Carrer de la Unió, a Sevillian family line and the Olivé group run an Andalusian bar where tortillitas de camarones come straight from the oil and jamón is carved within reach; MICHELIN lists it. At Cal Pep on Plaça de les Olles, open since 1989, there is no printed menu: the cooks decide and plate in sequence. Quimet & Quimet in Poble-sec, a family bodega since 1914, has no stools at all, and every montadito is built from the tins stacked on its walls.
counters.where: Bar Cañete on Carrer de la Unió; Cal Pep on Plaça de les Olles; Quimet & Quimet on Carrer del Poeta Cabanyes

sea.title: Fishermen's quarters, fishermen's food
sea.story: Barceloneta was laid out in the eighteenth century for fishermen and port workers, and Poblenou grew up beside the factories and the shore; their tables still cook for appetites like those. La Cova Fumada, a signless tavern from 1944, is where the grandmother of the house invented the bomba in the 1950s. El Vaso de Oro, opened in 1962, pours the family's own Fort beer and earns a Guía Repsol Solete for its solomillo con foie. In Poblenou, Els Pescadors has cooked rice and fish since 1980 in a fishermen's tavern dating to 1913, on a square shaded by ombú trees.
sea.where: La Cova Fumada on Carrer del Baluard; El Vaso de Oro on Carrer de Balboa; Els Pescadors on Plaça de Prim

vermut.title: The Sunday-noon vermut hour
vermut.story: In Barcelona 'fer el vermut' means a glass of sweet red vermut before lunch, usually at weekend noon, with tins and olives, and the bodegas that served it never stopped. El Xampanyet in El Born, opened in 1929, took its name from its own cloudy sparkling wine and is run by the founder's granddaughters. Bar Bodega Quimet in Gràcia kept its barrels and marble tables when the Montero brothers took over in 2010. Morro Fi began as a 2007 blog by three friends rating aperitiu bars, and opened its own standing bar on Consell de Cent in 2011.
vermut.where: El Xampanyet on Carrer de Montcada; Bar Bodega Quimet on Carrer de Vic; Morro Fi on Carrer del Consell de Cent

wine.title: Bottles off the wall
wine.story: Barcelona's wine rooms often blur shop and bar: you choose from the shelves and drink at close to retail price. Bar Mut, opened in June 2005 by Kim Díaz on Pau Claris, keeps more than 300 bottles behind a marble counter and writes its food on a daily chalkboard. Can Cisa and Bar Brutal in El Born opened in 2013 as one of the city's first natural-wine rooms, with Venetian twins Max and Stefano Colombo cooking. Els Sortidors del Parlament, in a former Sant Antoni motorbike workshop, sells bottles at shop price plus corkage, drunk over upturned barrels.
wine.where: Bar Mut on Carrer de Pau Claris; Can Cisa / Bar Brutal on Carrer de la Princesa; Els Sortidors del Parlament on Carrer del Parlament

granja.title: Thick chocolate, afternoon hour
granja.story: A granja was a dairy bar, selling milk, cream and curd cheese, and the survivors became the city's places for thick hot chocolate in the late afternoon. Granja M. Viader has traded on Carrer d'en Xuclà since 1870; the family patented Cacaolat there in 1931, and a fifth-generation owner took over in May 2026. Caelum, in the Gothic Quarter, sells sweets made in Spanish convents and serves chocolate in a vaulted basement over medieval baths. On La Rambla, Escribà runs a pastry counter in the 1902 modernista shopfront of the Antiga Casa Figueras.
granja.where: Granja M. Viader on Carrer d'en Xuclà; Caelum on Carrer de la Palla; Escribà on La Rambla

standing.title: One plate, decades deep
standing.story: Some Barcelona bars have served the same short list for generations and are crowded because of it. Bar La Plata, opened in 1945 near the port, offers four tapas only: fried small fish, anchovies, botifarra and a tomato salad, with barrel wine from Penedès. Can Paixano, since 1969 by Port Vell, pours its own pink cava to a crowd standing between hanging hams, with a botifarra roll from the grill. Up in Sarrià, Bar Tomás has served bravas since 1929 under allioli and chilli oil rather than red sauce, and Time Out ranks them among the city's best.
standing.where: Bar La Plata on Carrer de la Mercè; Can Paixano on Carrer de la Reina Cristina; Bar Tomás on Carrer Major de Sarrià

quick.title: Burgers and tortillas, fast
quick.story: The quick plate in Barcelona runs from the tortilla bar to the burger counter. Flash Flash, opened in 1970 by photographer Leopoldo Pomés with architect Alfonso Milà, serves more than fifty tortillas in a white room lined with silhouettes cut from Pomés's photographs of the model Karin Leiz; it is open late every day. Bacoa started in 2010 as a 15-seat counter behind the Santa Caterina market, where Brad Ainsworth grilled burgers over stone and won Time Out Barcelona's best-sandwich award; AmRest bought the chain in 2018 and the original site is listed closed.
quick.where: Flash Flash on Carrer de la Granada del Penedès; Bacoa Kiosko on Avinguda del Marquès de l'Argentera
